name: Bows, ramen & wrestling
why: The bow shop, then a famous spicy ramen, then two floors of pro wrestling goods in Sugamo. It is the day after Ryogoku, so you will have things to look for.
steps: Your hotel lobby
I pick you up. Kanda is about 10 minutes away.
Koyama Kyugu, Kanda main store
Bow maker for over 200 years, with its own workshop for bows, arrows and gloves. You can hold the bows and ask the staff anything. This is the main stop, so we take our time.
Early lunch at Kikanbo
Spicy miso ramen with chili and Sichuan pepper. We go before 12:00 to skip the line.
Train to Sugamo
About 20 minutes on the Yamanote line.
Toudoukan pro wrestling shop
Two floors of wrestling and MMA goods: masks, signed boards, old programs, DVDs and figures. One minute from the station.
Train to Daikanyama
About 40 minutes.
Daikanyama: Tsutaya Books and Log Road
Quiet streets, a big design bookshop and a garden path on an old rail line.
Done
At Daikanyama station, or I ride back with you.
moves: Hotel → Kanda about 10 min. Kanda → Sugamo about 20 min by train. Sugamo → Daikanyama about 40 min by train.
food: Red miso broth with chili and Sichuan pepper. You can ask for it milder.
Garden restaurant next to Tsutaya Books, for a second stop in the afternoon.
Bread, sandwiches and coffee on Log Road. Good for a short break outside.
good: The wrestling course. Toudoukan is open every day and sells things you will not find at the venue.
mind: Two train rides, about 20 and 40 minutes. Kikanbo is spicy, but you can ask for it milder.

name: Asakusa, and the river home
chips: Ends a few minutes from your hotel
why: You will have been awake since a quarter past four and had lunch already. This course is built so that the moving after that is done sitting down: a temple in the morning district, then a boat that carries you back down the Sumida and drops you almost at your door. Nothing here needs booking and nothing here is far.
steps: After lunch
About 25 minutes by train from Ginza to Asakusa. You can sleep on it.
Senso-ji, Asakusa

Tokyo’s oldest temple, founded in 628. You come in under a five-metre paper lantern, down a street of stalls selling rice crackers and fans that has been a shopping street for three hundred years. Flat the whole way, benches in the courtyard.
Something sweet on Nakamise
Melon bread straight out of the oven, or a bag of hot senbei. We eat as we walk back to the pier.
The boat down the Sumida
Forty minutes on the water. Twelve bridges, each one a different colour, the Skytree behind you and the city sliding past. You are sitting the whole way and there is a toilet on board.
Hama-rikyu Gardens
The boat lands inside a 400-year-old shogun’s garden with saltwater ponds. Flat gravel paths, benches all the way round, the skyline standing over the pines.
Tea over the pond, if you want it
A tea house on stilts out over the water. Matcha whisked in front of you with a seasonal sweet. Entirely optional.
Back at the hotel
Fifteen minutes on foot, or one short taxi.
moves: Hotel → Asakusa about 25 min by train. Temple on foot. Pier is 5 min from the temple. Boat to Hama-rikyu 40 min. Garden → hotel 15 min on foot.
food: Frying the same dark sesame-oil tempura since 1887. Prawns over rice in a lacquer bowl. There is usually a queue and it moves.
Beef cooked at your table in a shallow iron pan, dipped in raw egg. Founded 1895, and the room is quiet and seated.
Melon bread, grilled rice crackers, sweet bean cakes shaped like the temple gate. A few hundred yen each, eaten standing.
good: The most rest per hour of the three. Almost all of the distance is covered sitting on a boat or a train, and you finish within walking distance of your bed.
mind: The last boat of the day leaves in the late afternoon, so this course cannot start much later than 13:00. If the weather turns, the boat still runs — the deck is covered.
